questions.question: Who sang 'Mona Lisa' in 1950?
questions.fact: It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.question: Patti Page's huge 1950 hit was a waltz named after which state?
questions.fact: 'Tennessee Waltz' became one of the best-selling records of its time, and Tennessee later made it an official state song.

questions.question: In the early 1950s, a new sound mixed country with rhythm and blues. What was it called?
questions.fact: Rock and roll grew out of blues, country and gospel. By 1955, Chuck Berry and Little Richard were bringing the new sound to the whole country.

questions.question: Vaughn Monroe's 'Riders in the Sky' was a huge 1949 hit. What kind of song was it?
questions.fact: Its ghostly cowboys have been recorded by many artists since, from Bing Crosby to Johnny Cash.

questions.question: Which crooner had a No. 1 hit with 'Till the End of Time' in 1945?
questions.fact: Its melody was borrowed from a famous piano piece by Chopin, his 'Polonaise in A-flat major.'

questions.question: Which singer had her first big hit with 'Sentimental Journey' in 1945?
questions.fact: She recorded it with Les Brown and his band. It became a homecoming song for soldiers returning from the war.

questions.question: Which sister group recorded the 1945 hit 'Rum and Coca-Cola'?
questions.fact: It topped the charts for weeks, even though some radio networks refused to play it because it named a brand.

questions.question: Perry Como had a No. 1 hit in 1946 with which romantic ballad?
questions.fact: The song was first made popular in 1931 by Russ Columbo, a crooner who helped write it.

questions.question: Columbia Records introduced a new kind of record in 1948 that could hold a whole album. What was it?
questions.fact: It spun at 33 1/3 turns a minute. An old 78 held only about three to five minutes a side.

questions.question: Francis Craig's 'Near You' was the big hit of 1947. How many weeks did it spend at No. 1?
questions.fact: It spent 17 weeks in a row at No. 1 on the disc jockeys' chart, a record that stood for over 60 years. It later became Milton Berle's TV theme song.

questions.question: The Harmonicats had a surprise 1947 hit with which old tune played on harmonicas?
questions.fact: The song was already more than 30 years old. It was written in 1913 for a Broadway show.

questions.question: Which entertainer had a 1947 comeback hit with 'Anniversary Song' from a movie about his own life?
questions.fact: The movie was 'The Jolson Story.' Larry Parks played Jolson on screen, but Jolson sang the songs himself.

questions.question: Which singer of the 1940s was nicknamed 'The Voice'?
questions.fact: Teenage bobby-soxers screamed and swooned at his shows at the Paramount in New York.

questions.question: Dinah Shore's 'Buttons and Bows' topped the charts in 1948. Which Bob Hope film was it from?
questions.fact: Bob Hope sang it in the movie. It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.question: Nat King Cole was a star singer by 1948. Which instrument was he also famous for playing?
questions.fact: He started out as a jazz pianist leading the King Cole Trio. His singing soon made him a pop star.

questions.question: Perry Como's 1949 hit 'Some Enchanted Evening' came from which Broadway musical?
questions.fact: 'South Pacific' won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, a rare honor for a musical.

questions.question: Which folk group had a giant hit in 1950 with 'Goodnight, Irene'?
questions.fact: The song came from the blues singer Lead Belly. Pete Seeger was one of the Weavers.

questions.question: Which Les Paul and Mary Ford record spent nine weeks at No. 1 in 1951?
questions.fact: Les Paul stacked many guitar and voice parts on tape, a recording trick he helped pioneer.

questions.question: Who recorded the 1951 hit 'Too Young'?
questions.fact: Billboard named it the top song of 1951.

questions.question: Pop star Eddie Fisher got his own TV show in 1953. Which drink company sponsored it?
questions.fact: The show was called 'Coke Time with Eddie Fisher.' It ran on NBC until 1957.

questions.question: Vera Lynn, the 'Forces' Sweetheart' of the war years, had a US No. 1 in 1952 with which song?
questions.fact: It was the first record by a singer from outside the US to reach No. 1 on the American charts.

questions.question: In Patti Page's 1953 hit, where was the doggie she wanted to buy?
questions.fact: The record has a dog barking along with Patti. The barks were done by two people, billed on the label as 'Joe and Mac.'

questions.question: Who sang the 1953 country hit 'Your Cheatin' Heart'?
questions.fact: It topped the country chart in 1953 and has been recorded by hundreds of singers since, from Patsy Cline to Ray Charles.

questions.question: A young truck driver recorded 'That's All Right' at Sun Studio in Memphis in 1954. Who was he?
questions.fact: He was just 19. A Memphis disc jockey played the record over and over on the night it first aired.

questions.question: Which bandleader first recorded 'Rock Around the Clock' in 1954?
questions.fact: It became a smash in 1955, after it played over the opening of the movie 'Blackboard Jungle.'

questions.question: Hank Williams had a 1952 hit about a Cajun party on the bayou. What was it called?
questions.fact: The song name-checks crawfish pie and filé gumbo. Jo Stafford and, much later, the Carpenters both had hits with it.

questions.question: Rosemary Clooney's 1951 hit invited everyone to 'come on-a' where?
questions.fact: 'Come On-a My House' was co-written by Ross Bagdasarian, who later created Alvin and the Chipmunks.

questions.question: Singing cowboy Gene Autry's 1949 Christmas hit was about which reindeer?
questions.fact: Rudolph was created in 1939 for a Montgomery Ward booklet. The song's writer, Johnny Marks, was the creator's brother-in-law.

questions.question: Which crooner sang the 1953 hit 'That's Amore'?
questions.fact: He sang it in 'The Caddy,' a comedy with his partner Jerry Lewis. It was nominated for an Academy Award.

questions.question: Which singer, who later left his heart in San Francisco, had his first No. 1 hit in 1951?
questions.fact: His first No. 1 was 'Because of You.' He followed it the same year with 'Cold, Cold Heart.'

questions.question: In the 1948 Christmas novelty song, what did the singer want for Christmas?
questions.fact: Spike Jones and His City Slickers had the hit. George Rock sang it in a little-boy voice.

questions.question: In the Chordettes' 1954 hit, what did they ask Mr. Sandman to bring them?
questions.fact: Vaughn Monroe recorded it first, earlier in 1954, but the Chordettes' barbershop-style harmony made theirs the big hit.

questions.question: Which trumpet player and singer was nicknamed 'Satchmo'?
questions.fact: In 1947 he started a small band called the All Stars, which he led for the rest of his career.

questions.question: In 'The Christmas Song,' first recorded by Nat King Cole in 1946, what is roasting on an open fire?
questions.fact: Mel Tormé and Bob Wells wrote it on a hot summer day in 1945, trying to 'stay cool by thinking cool.'

questions.question: Finish the title of Eileen Barton's 1950 hit: 'If I Knew You Were Comin' I'd've…'
questions.fact: The bouncy song made Eileen Barton a star. She had been performing on radio since she was a small child.

questions.question: Which Broadway musical of 1946 introduced 'There's No Business Like Show Business'?
questions.fact: Ethel Merman starred as sharpshooter Annie Oakley. Irving Berlin wrote the songs.

questions.question: Which 1951 Broadway musical gave us the song 'Getting to Know You'?
questions.fact: Yul Brynner played the King on Broadway, and won an Academy Award when he played him again in the 1956 film.

questions.question: Who sang 'You Belong to Me,' the No. 1 hit about seeing the pyramids along the Nile, in 1952?
questions.fact: Her record also topped the British chart. She was the first woman ever to reach No. 1 there.

questions.question: Kay Starr's 1952 No. 1 hit hoped which 'wheel' would turn her way?
questions.fact: 'Wheel of Fortune' stayed at No. 1 for ten weeks and was Kay Starr's biggest hit.

questions.question: A comedy routine became a 1947 hit song. Who was asked to 'open the door'?
questions.fact: 'Open the Door, Richard' came from a vaudeville comedy act. Count Basie's version went to No. 1.

questions.question: Which 1950 Broadway musical featured gamblers and the song 'Luck Be a Lady'?
questions.fact: It was based on Damon Runyon's stories of Broadway characters, and won the Tony Award for Best Musical.

questions.question: Which emotional singer was nicknamed 'the Prince of Wails' after his 1951 hit 'Cry'?
questions.fact: He often wept on stage. 'Cry' spent 11 weeks at No. 1.

questions.question: Which singer had a No. 1 hit in early 1954 with the tender song 'Oh! My Pa-Pa'?
questions.fact: It began as a German song by a Swiss composer, sung by a young woman remembering her father, a famous clown.

questions.question: Which singer, nicknamed 'The Velvet Fog,' co-wrote 'The Christmas Song' in 1945?
questions.fact: He was only 19 at the time. Nat King Cole's recording made the song a holiday classic.

questions.question: Which 1953 Broadway musical gave us 'Stranger in Paradise'?
questions.fact: Its music was borrowed from the Russian composer Alexander Borodin, written about 80 years earlier.

questions.question: Frankie Laine's 1949 hit 'Mule Train' was famous for what sound?
questions.fact: Several singers had hits with 'Mule Train' at the same time, including Bing Crosby, but Frankie Laine's sold best.

questions.question: Which doo-wop group sang 'Earth Angel' in 1954?
questions.fact: It was recorded in a garage in Los Angeles and became one of the first rhythm and blues records to cross over to the pop charts.

questions.question: The Mills Brothers' 1952 hit was about which glowing insect?
questions.fact: 'The Glow-Worm' began as a German song from 1902. Johnny Mercer wrote new words for the Mills Brothers.

questions.question: Which singer had a 1948 No. 1 hit with 'Mañana (Is Soon Enough for Me)'?
questions.fact: She wrote it with her husband, guitarist Dave Barbour. It stayed at No. 1 for nine weeks.

questions.question: Rosemary Clooney's 1954 No. 1 'Hey There' came from which Broadway musical?
questions.fact: In the show, a man records his thoughts on a dictating machine, then plays the tape back and sings a duet with himself.

questions.question: Which hit 1951 comedy starred Lucille Ball?
questions.fact: Lucy and Desi filmed it in front of a live audience with three cameras, a method sitcoms still use today.

questions.question: Which children's show of 1947 starred a freckle-faced cowboy puppet?
questions.fact: Buffalo Bob Smith was the host, and the kids in the studio audience sat in the 'Peanut Gallery.'

questions.question: What was the main source of home entertainment for most American families in 1945?
questions.fact: Families gathered around the radio every evening for comedies, music and news, just as they later gathered around the TV.

questions.question: Which comedian was nicknamed 'Mr. Television' in the late 1940s?
questions.fact: His Tuesday night show, the 'Texaco Star Theater,' was so popular that people bought TV sets just to watch him.

questions.question: Which early TV network competed with NBC and CBS but shut down in 1956?
questions.fact: DuMont was one of the first TV networks, but it could not keep up with its bigger rivals.

questions.question: NBC's 'Hour Glass' of 1946 was one of TV's first big entertainment shows. What kind of show was it?
questions.fact: It mixed singers, comedians and dancers, a recipe that early TV used again and again.

questions.question: The 1947 World Series was the first one shown on TV. Which two New York teams played?
questions.fact: Only a few cities could see it, including New York, Philadelphia and Washington. The Yankees won in seven games.

questions.question: Which NBC news program began in 1947 and is still on the air today?
questions.fact: It is the longest-running program in American television history.

questions.question: Ed Sullivan's famous Sunday night variety show began in 1948 under what name?
questions.fact: It was renamed 'The Ed Sullivan Show' in 1955 and ran for 23 years.

questions.question: Which masked Western hero rode onto ABC television in 1949?
questions.fact: Clayton Moore played the masked man. A secret silver mine paid his way and supplied his famous silver bullets.

questions.question: Which family sitcom, a radio hit since 1929, came to TV in 1949 with Gertrude Berg as Molly?
questions.fact: Gertrude Berg created, wrote and starred in the show. She won the first Emmy ever given for best actress.

questions.question: Sid Caesar and Imogene Coca starred in which live comedy show that began in 1950?
questions.fact: Its writers included Mel Brooks, Carl Reiner and Neil Simon, who all became famous in their own right.

questions.question: Jack Benny brought his radio show to TV in 1950. What age did he always claim to be?
questions.fact: Benny played a vain penny-pincher who stayed 39 for decades and played the violin badly on purpose.

questions.question: In September 1951, President Truman's speech became the first live TV broadcast seen in what way?
questions.fact: He opened a peace conference in San Francisco, and viewers from coast to coast watched it live.

questions.question: What was the name of the stone-faced detective on TV's 'Dragnet,' which began in 1951?
questions.fact: Jack Webb created the show and starred as Sergeant Friday, badge number 714.

questions.question: 'Bandstand' began on Philadelphia TV in 1952. Who was its first host?
questions.fact: Dick Clark took over in 1956 and made it the national hit 'American Bandstand.'

questions.question: The 'Today' show premiered on NBC in January 1952. Who was its first host?
questions.fact: A chimpanzee named J. Fred Muggs became one of the show's most popular regulars.

questions.question: Which 1950s comedy featured bus driver Ralph Kramden and his wife Alice?
questions.fact: It began as sketches on Jackie Gleason's variety show. Art Carney played Ralph's pal Ed Norton, a sewer worker.

questions.question: Whose baby son was on the cover of the very first TV Guide in April 1953?
questions.fact: The cover showed little Desi Arnaz Jr. under the headline 'Lucy's $50,000,000 Baby.'

questions.question: Danny Thomas starred as a nightclub entertainer in which family sitcom that began in 1953?
questions.fact: It was later renamed 'The Danny Thomas Show.' An episode in 1960 introduced Andy Griffith as Sheriff Andy Taylor.

questions.question: Which comedian and songwriter launched NBC's late-night 'Tonight Show' in September 1954?
questions.fact: Steve Allen mixed comedy, music and chats with the audience. He also wrote thousands of songs.

questions.question: What was the name of the weekly TV show Walt Disney launched on ABC in 1954?
questions.fact: It shared its name with the theme park Walt was building. ABC helped pay for the park, which opened in July 1955.

questions.question: On TV's 'Burns and Allen,' which began in 1950, who played George Burns's scatterbrained wife?
questions.fact: George and Gracie were married in real life, and had played the same comedy team on radio for years.

questions.question: In a famous 1952 'I Love Lucy' episode, Lucy and Ethel work in a factory wrapping what?
questions.fact: The conveyor belt sped up, so they stuffed the candies in their mouths, hats and blouses. The episode is called 'Job Switching.'

questions.question: On 'I Love Lucy,' which began in 1951, what was the name of Lucy's bandleader husband?
questions.fact: Desi Arnaz played Ricky, who led the band at New York's Tropicana nightclub.

questions.question: On 'The Roy Rogers Show,' which began in 1951, what was the name of Roy's golden horse?
questions.fact: Trigger was billed as 'the Smartest Horse in the Movies.' Roy's wife, Dale Evans, rode a horse named Buttermilk.

questions.question: On Groucho Marx's quiz show 'You Bet Your Life,' what dropped down if a guest said the secret word?
questions.fact: The duck looked like Groucho, with glasses and a mustache, and brought a $100 bonus. The show came to TV in 1950.

questions.question: Which brave and loyal collie got her own TV show in 1954?
questions.fact: Lassie was a girl, but she was always played by male collies, starting with a dog named Pal and then his offspring.

questions.question: Which real-life family played themselves on 'The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet,' on TV from 1952?
questions.fact: Their younger son, Ricky Nelson, sang on the show and became a teen rock and roll idol.

questions.question: George Reeves played which hero in a TV series that began in 1952?
questions.fact: He was 'faster than a speeding bullet.' Later seasons were filmed in color, even though few families had color sets.

questions.question: On the panel show 'What's My Line?', which began in 1950, what did the panel try to guess?
questions.fact: Blindfolded panelists also tried to name a famous mystery guest. The show ran on CBS until 1967.

questions.question: Which TV comedian's catchphrase was 'And away we go!'?
questions.fact: He was nicknamed 'The Great One.' His variety show moved to CBS in 1952.

questions.question: On TV's 'The Lone Ranger' (1949), what was the name of the Ranger's loyal companion?
questions.fact: Jay Silverheels played Tonto. He was a Mohawk actor from Canada.

questions.question: 'The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin' began in 1954. What kind of dog was Rin Tin Tin?
questions.fact: The first Rin Tin Tin was a puppy found in France in 1918, near the end of World War I. He grew up to star in silent films.

questions.question: Which comedy team was famous for the 'Who's on First?' routine, seen on their own TV show from 1952?
questions.fact: Bud Abbott and Lou Costello had performed the baseball routine since the 1930s. It is in the Baseball Hall of Fame.

questions.question: In a famous 1952 'I Love Lucy' episode, Lucy gets tipsy filming a commercial for which tonic?
questions.fact: With every spoonful she took, the tonic's alcohol made her more wobbly. The episode is called 'Lucy Does a TV Commercial.'

questions.question: On TV's 'Kukla, Fran and Ollie,' what kind of creature was Ollie?
questions.fact: Puppeteer Burr Tillstrom worked every puppet himself, while Fran Allison chatted with them unscripted.

questions.question: TV cowboy Hopalong Cassidy, a hit with children from 1949, always dressed in what color?
questions.fact: William Boyd played Hoppy on his white horse, Topper. Children bought millions of Hopalong lunch boxes, cap guns and outfits.

questions.question: Which TV comedian, on the air from 1951, created the hobo clown Freddie the Freeloader?
questions.fact: He ended every show with 'Good night, and may God bless.' He was also a talented painter of clowns.

questions.question: Which big-nosed comedian ended his 1950s TV shows with 'Good night, Mrs. Calabash, wherever you are'?
questions.fact: He was nicknamed 'the Schnozzola.' He never explained who Mrs. Calabash was.

questions.question: Which actor played the dad, Jim Anderson, on 'Father Knows Best,' which came to TV in 1954?
questions.fact: He had played the same role on the radio version since 1949. Later he starred as TV's 'Marcus Welby, M.D.'

questions.question: On New Year's Day 1954, which parade became the first program broadcast in color across the country?
questions.fact: NBC sent the Pasadena parade to stations nationwide, though very few people owned a color set to see it.

questions.question: Which bishop's TV talks, 'Life Is Worth Living,' rivaled Milton Berle in the ratings starting in 1952?
questions.fact: He spoke with a chalkboard and no script, and won an Emmy in 1953.

questions.question: Marlin Perkins hosted which 1950s animal show from Chicago's Lincoln Park Zoo?
questions.fact: He later hosted 'Mutual of Omaha's Wild Kingdom,' which began in 1963.

questions.question: On the children's show 'Romper Room,' which began in 1953, well-behaved children were called what?
questions.fact: Badly behaved ones were 'Don't Bees.' At the end, the teacher looked through her Magic Mirror and named children at home.

questions.question: On 'Our Miss Brooks,' which came to TV in 1952, what was Connie Brooks's job?
questions.fact: Eve Arden played the wisecracking teacher at Madison High School, on radio first and then on TV.

questions.question: On 'Howdy Doody,' Clarabell the Clown never spoke. How did Clarabell 'talk'?
questions.fact: Clarabell also squirted a seltzer bottle. Bob Keeshan, the first Clarabell, later became TV's Captain Kangaroo.

questions.question: Which future president began hosting TV's 'General Electric Theater' in 1954?
questions.fact: He introduced the weekly dramas for eight years and toured GE factories giving speeches.

questions.question: Which singer closed her 1950s TV shows by blowing a big kiss after singing 'See the USA in Your Chevrolet'?
questions.fact: Chevrolet sponsored her show, and the jingle became one of the best-known in TV history.

questions.question: On TV's 'The Cisco Kid,' which began in 1950, what was the name of Cisco's jolly sidekick?
questions.fact: It was one of the first TV series filmed in color, years before most families could watch in color.

questions.question: Who played George Bailey in 1946's 'It's a Wonderful Life'?
questions.fact: Jimmy Stewart called it his favorite film. It did poorly at first, then became a Christmas classic once TV stations began showing it every year.

questions.question: Which 1947 movie features a kind old man named Kris Kringle who says he is the real Santa Claus?
questions.fact: Edmund Gwenn won an Academy Award for playing Kris. The studio released the film in May, worried a Christmas movie would not sell.

questions.question: Which 1950 Disney movie featured a glass slipper and a fairy godmother?
questions.fact: The Fairy Godmother's song 'Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo' became one of Disney's best-known tunes.

questions.question: Which 1951 film had Humphrey Bogart and Katharine Hepburn on a rickety boat down an African river?
questions.fact: It won Bogart his only Academy Award. Much of it was filmed on location in Africa, a hard trip for the cast and crew.

questions.question: Gene Kelly danced through a rainstorm in which 1952 musical?
questions.fact: The film pokes fun at Hollywood's switch from silent movies to talkies in the late 1920s.

questions.question: Gary Cooper played a marshal facing a gang of outlaws alone in which 1952 Western?
questions.fact: Cooper won the Academy Award for Best Actor. The story unfolds in almost real time, with clocks ticking toward noon.

questions.question: In Alfred Hitchcock's 1954 'Rear Window,' who played the photographer spying on his neighbors?
questions.fact: His character is stuck in a wheelchair with a broken leg, so the whole film is seen from his apartment. Grace Kelly played his girlfriend.

questions.question: Which 1954 Bing Crosby and Danny Kaye musical was the year's biggest box-office hit?
questions.fact: It was the first film made in VistaVision, a sharp new widescreen process. Rosemary Clooney and Vera-Ellen co-starred.

questions.question: Laurence Olivier directed and starred in which Shakespeare film that won Best Picture for 1948?
questions.fact: It was the first British film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Olivier also won Best Actor.

questions.question: Which 1950 film ends with the famous line 'All right, Mr. DeMille, I'm ready for my close-up'?
questions.fact: Gloria Swanson played a faded silent-movie star, and she really had been one of the biggest silent stars.

questions.question: Which 1950 film set a record with 14 Academy Award nominations?
questions.fact: Bette Davis starred, and it won Best Picture. Its record stood for decades and was tied by 'Titanic' and 'La La Land.'

questions.question: Which 1951 Gene Kelly musical, set in France, won the Academy Award for Best Picture?
questions.fact: It ends with a dazzling ballet that runs about 17 minutes, set to music by George Gershwin.

questions.question: Marlon Brando played Stanley Kowalski in which 1951 drama based on a Tennessee Williams play?
questions.fact: Vivien Leigh, Kim Hunter and Karl Malden all won Academy Awards for it. Brando was nominated but did not win.

questions.question: Which 1953 Western ends with young Joey calling after a gunfighter, 'Come back!'?
questions.fact: Alan Ladd played the quiet stranger who helps a farm family. It was filmed in Wyoming, with the Grand Tetons behind.

questions.question: Which 1953 film, set in Rome, made Audrey Hepburn a star and won her the Oscar for Best Actress?
questions.fact: She played a princess who slips away to explore Rome with a reporter, played by Gregory Peck.

questions.question: Burt Lancaster and Deborah Kerr's famous kiss in the surf is from which 1953 Best Picture winner?
questions.fact: It won eight Academy Awards, including one for Frank Sinatra, which revived his career.

questions.question: Which 1954 Marlon Brando film has the line 'I coulda been a contender'?
questions.fact: Brando won Best Actor, and the film won eight Academy Awards in all, including Best Picture.

questions.question: Gregory Peck and Ingrid Bergman starred in which 1945 Alfred Hitchcock thriller?
questions.fact: The famous artist Salvador Dalí designed its strange dream scenes.

questions.question: Which 1946 Best Picture winner told of three servicemen coming home after the war?
options: The Best Years of Our Lives
questions.fact: Harold Russell, a real veteran who had never acted, won two Oscars for the same role.

questions.question: Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall starred together in which 1947 thriller?
questions.fact: They met making To Have and Have Not, married in 1945, and made four films together.

questions.question: Jane Wyman won Best Actress for playing a young deaf woman in which 1948 film?
questions.fact: She studied sign language for the part and does not speak a word on screen.

questions.question: Which 1948 British film about a young ballerina became a big hit in America?
questions.fact: Director Martin Scorsese has called it one of the greatest films ever made.

questions.question: Olivia de Havilland won Best Actress for 1949's 'The Heiress.' Who directed it?
questions.fact: It was her second Oscar. Aaron Copland also won an Academy Award for the film's music.

questions.question: Which 1949 film about a power-hungry Southern politician won the Best Picture Oscar?
questions.fact: It was based on a Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, and Broderick Crawford won Best Actor as Willie Stark.

questions.question: Cecil B. DeMille's circus movie won Best Picture for 1952. What was it called?
questions.fact: 'Singin' in the Rain' came out the same year and was not even nominated for Best Picture.

questions.question: In Disney's 1951 'Alice in Wonderland,' who throws the mad tea party?
questions.fact: He and the March Hare sing 'The Unbirthday Song,' celebrating every day that isn't your birthday.

questions.question: In Disney's 1953 'Peter Pan,' what is the name of Peter's little fairy friend?
questions.fact: She never speaks a word. Her voice is the sound of tinkling bells.

questions.question: In 1953's 'Gentlemen Prefer Blondes,' Marilyn Monroe sang that what are a girl's best friend?
questions.fact: Jane Russell co-starred. Marilyn's pink gown in that number became one of the most famous costumes in film.

questions.question: In 1952's 'The Quiet Man,' John Wayne goes back to which country, where he was born?
questions.fact: Maureen O'Hara co-starred, and John Ford won the Academy Award for Best Director for it.

questions.question: Who danced with Judy Garland in the 1948 musical 'Easter Parade'?
questions.fact: Gene Kelly was supposed to star, but he broke his ankle. Fred Astaire came out of retirement to take his place.

questions.question: In 1949's 'On the Town,' Gene Kelly and Frank Sinatra play sailors on leave in which city?
questions.fact: It was one of the first Hollywood musicals to film scenes on real city streets instead of a studio lot.

questions.question: In 1950's 'Harvey,' James Stewart's invisible best friend is a giant what?
questions.fact: Harvey is a 'pooka,' a spirit from Irish folklore, and stands over six feet tall. The story began as a Broadway play.

questions.question: Spencer Tracy played the worried dad in 1950's 'Father of the Bride.' Who played the bride?
questions.fact: She was only 18. Just 12 days before the premiere, she married hotel heir Nicky Hilton in real life.

questions.question: What was Captain Nemo's submarine called in Disney's 1954 '20,000 Leagues Under the Sea'?
questions.fact: Kirk Douglas starred, and James Mason played Nemo. The film's giant squid fight helped it win an Oscar for special effects.

questions.question: In 1945's 'Anchors Aweigh,' Gene Kelly dances with which famous cartoon mouse?
questions.fact: Jerry, of Tom and Jerry, was drawn in frame by frame to match Kelly's steps. Frank Sinatra co-starred.

questions.question: In 1948's 'The Treasure of the Sierra Madre,' what are Humphrey Bogart and his partners digging for?
questions.fact: John Huston directed his own father, Walter Huston, and both won Academy Awards for the film.

questions.question: Doris Day played which Wild West heroine in a 1953 musical?
questions.fact: Her song from the film, 'Secret Love,' won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

questions.question: In 1947's 'The Bishop's Wife,' what does Cary Grant play?
questions.fact: His angel, Dudley, comes to help a bishop, played by David Niven, and his wife, played by Loretta Young.

questions.question: Which 1953 Bible epic was the first movie released in widescreen CinemaScope?
questions.fact: Richard Burton starred. Theaters installed wide, curved screens to show it, hoping to lure viewers away from TV.

questions.question: Which 1953 Vincent Price thriller was a big hit in 3-D?
questions.fact: Its director, André de Toth, was blind in one eye, so he could not see the 3-D effects himself.

questions.question: In 1951's 'The Day the Earth Stood Still,' what is the name of the giant silver robot?
questions.fact: The spaceman Klaatu gives the famous order to stop him: 'Klaatu barada nikto.'

questions.question: In 1954's 'Sabrina,' Audrey Hepburn plays the daughter of a rich family's what?
questions.fact: Humphrey Bogart and William Holden played the two brothers who fall for her.

questions.question: The 1954 musical 'Seven Brides for Seven Brothers' is set in the backwoods of which state?
questions.fact: Its barn-raising dance, with the brothers leaping over beams and sawhorses, is one of the most famous dances on film.

questions.question: In 1954's 'The Caine Mutiny,' what does Captain Queeg nervously roll in his hand?
questions.fact: Humphrey Bogart played Queeg. He also obsessed over a quart of missing strawberries.

questions.question: In 1949's 'Adam's Rib,' Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn play a married couple with what job?
questions.fact: They end up on opposite sides of the same court case. It was one of nine films they made together.

questions.question: In 1946's 'The Big Sleep,' Humphrey Bogart plays which famous private detective?
questions.fact: The story came from a Raymond Chandler novel, and the plot is so twisty that even the writers were confused.

questions.question: In 1946's 'The Yearling,' what pet does young Jody raise on his family's Florida farm?
questions.fact: Claude Jarman Jr., who played Jody, was given a special Academy Award as the year's outstanding child actor.

questions.question: Which 1954 film gave Judy Garland the torch song 'The Man That Got Away'?
questions.fact: James Mason co-starred. It was her first movie in four years, and both stars were nominated for Academy Awards.

questions.question: In the 1954 musical 'Brigadoon,' the magical Scottish village appears for one day every how many years?
questions.fact: Gene Kelly and Cyd Charisse starred. Scotland's weather and costs ruled out filming there, so the highlands were built on MGM sound stages.

questions.question: Danny Kaye played which famous Danish storyteller in a 1952 musical?
questions.fact: The film's songs include 'Thumbelina,' 'The Inch Worm' and 'Wonderful Copenhagen.'

questions.question: Jackie Robinson broke baseball's color line in 1947. Which team did he play for?
questions.fact: Today every Major League player wears his number, 42, on Jackie Robinson Day each April.

questions.question: Which boxer, nicknamed 'The Brown Bomber,' was heavyweight champion for most of the 1940s?
questions.fact: He held the title from 1937 until he retired in 1949, the longest reign of any heavyweight champion.

questions.question: After winning Olympic gold in track, which sport did Babe Didrikson Zaharias rule in the late 1940s?
questions.fact: She won ten major golf championships and helped found the LPGA, the women's pro golf tour, in 1950.

questions.question: In 1954, Roger Bannister became the first person to run a mile in under how many minutes?
questions.fact: He ran it in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds on May 6, 1954, in Oxford, England. He was a medical student at the time.

questions.question: Willie Mays made his big-league debut in 1951. Which team did he play for?
questions.fact: He started with just one hit in his first 26 at-bats. His manager stuck with him, and he was named Rookie of the Year.

questions.question: Which St. Louis Cardinals slugger won the National League MVP award in 1946?
questions.fact: He won the MVP award three times, in 1943, 1946 and 1948, and played his whole career for St. Louis.

questions.question: Jackie Robinson won which award in his first big-league season, 1947?
questions.fact: It was the first year the award was given. In 1987 it was renamed the Jackie Robinson Award.

questions.question: The 1948 Summer Olympics in London were the first since 1936. Which country won the most gold medals?
questions.fact: They were called the 'Austerity Games,' because Britain was still rationing food. Athletes stayed in schools and army camps.

questions.question: Who managed the New York Yankees to the 1949 World Series title in his first year with the team?
questions.fact: 'The Ol' Perfessor' was known for his twisted way of talking, called 'Stengelese.' His Yankees won five titles in a row.

questions.question: In 1950, Florence Chadwick swam which famous body of water faster than any woman before her?
questions.fact: She swam from France to England in 13 hours and 20 minutes, beating Gertrude Ederle's record from 1926.

questions.question: Bobby Thomson's 1951 'Shot Heard Round the World' won the pennant for the Giants. Which team did it beat?
questions.fact: Giants radio announcer Russ Hodges shouted 'The Giants win the pennant!' over and over.

questions.question: Rocky Marciano won the heavyweight title in 1952. What was his record when he retired?
questions.fact: He is the only heavyweight champion to retire without ever losing a professional fight.

questions.question: Golfer Ben Hogan won three major titles in 1953. What had he survived four years earlier?
questions.fact: In 1949 his car hit a Greyhound bus head-on. Doctors feared he might not walk again, but he came back to win six more majors.

questions.question: Willie Mays made an amazing over-the-shoulder grab in the 1954 World Series. What is it simply called?
questions.fact: He ran down Vic Wertz's long drive at the Polo Grounds. The Giants went on to sweep Cleveland in four games.

questions.question: The St. Louis Cardinals won a thrilling 7-game World Series in 1946. Who did they beat?
questions.fact: Enos Slaughter's famous 'Mad Dash' home from first base in Game 7 won it for St. Louis.

questions.question: The Yankees beat the Dodgers in the 1952 World Series. How many titles in a row was that for New York?
questions.fact: The Yankees won five World Series in a row, from 1949 to 1953, under manager Casey Stengel.

questions.question: Which country won soccer's 1954 World Cup?
questions.fact: West Germany upset heavily favored Hungary 3 to 2 in what became known as the 'Miracle of Bern.'

questions.question: Which team beat the Chicago Cubs in the 1945 World Series?
questions.fact: The Cubs would not play in another World Series for 71 years, until they won it all in 2016.

questions.question: The Cleveland Rams won the NFL title in 1945, then moved in 1946. Where did they go?
questions.fact: They became the first major-league sports team based on the West Coast.

questions.question: Citation won horse racing's Triple Crown in 1948. Who was his famous jockey?
questions.fact: He also won the Triple Crown on Whirlaway in 1941. He is still the only jockey to win it twice.

questions.question: Cleveland won the 1948 World Series with which shortstop as its player-manager?
questions.fact: He batted .355 that year and was named the American League's Most Valuable Player.

questions.question: Joe Louis retired as heavyweight champion in 1949. How many times had he defended the title?
questions.fact: His 25 successful title defenses are still the most by any heavyweight champion.

questions.question: The young 1950 Philadelphia Phillies won the National League pennant. What was their nickname?
questions.fact: Young stars like pitcher Robin Roberts and outfielder Richie Ashburn led the way. The Yankees swept them in the World Series.

questions.question: In a famous 1950 World Cup upset, the United States soccer team beat which country 1 to 0?
questions.fact: The Americans were mostly part-timers. Some English newspapers were said to think the score was a misprint.

questions.question: Which American won the Olympic decathlon in both 1948 and 1952?
questions.fact: He was only 17 when he won in 1948, and later served in Congress.

questions.question: Which Yankee star, who retired after the 1951 season, was nicknamed 'The Yankee Clipper'?
questions.fact: His 56-game hitting streak from 1941 is still a record. In 1954 he married Marilyn Monroe.

questions.question: Which Yankee catcher, famous for sayings like 'It ain't over till it's over,' was the 1951 AL MVP?
questions.fact: He won the MVP award three times and played on ten World Series champions.

questions.question: Which Yankee legend, 'The Bambino,' was honored in 1948 when the team retired his number 3?
questions.fact: He hit 714 home runs in his career, a record that stood until 1974.

questions.question: Which Boston Red Sox slugger, the 1946 AL MVP, was nicknamed 'The Splendid Splinter'?
questions.fact: In 1941 he batted .406. No major leaguer has hit .400 for a season since.

questions.question: George Mikan, the first great 'big man,' led the Minneapolis Lakers to titles in which sport?
questions.fact: He stood 6 feet 10 and wore thick glasses on the court. The league widened the lane under the basket partly because of him.

questions.question: The Toronto Maple Leafs won hockey's top prize in 1947, 1948 and 1949. What is it called?
questions.fact: They were the first team to win the Stanley Cup three years in a row.

questions.question: Which Detroit Red Wings star of the early 1950s was nicknamed 'Mr. Hockey'?
questions.fact: He played professional hockey in five different decades, retiring for good at age 52.

questions.question: Which weekly sports magazine published its very first issue in August 1954?
questions.fact: It came from the publishers of Time and Life magazines and ran as a weekly for more than 60 years.

questions.question: Sugar Ray Robinson, often called the best fighter of all time, was a champion in which sport?
questions.fact: He won the middleweight title five times, the first in 1951. Muhammad Ali called him his idol.

questions.question: What did Brooklyn Dodgers fans fondly call their team in the early 1950s?
questions.fact: After each World Series loss to the Yankees, fans cried 'Wait 'til next year!' Next year finally came in 1955.

questions.question: Which future home run king made his big-league debut with the Milwaukee Braves in 1954?
questions.fact: Twenty years later, in 1974, he broke Babe Ruth's career record of 714 home runs.

questions.question: Gorgeous George, with his golden curls and perfumed valet, was a TV star of which sport?
questions.fact: He strutted to the ring to 'Pomp and Circumstance.' Young Muhammad Ali later copied his showmanship.

questions.question: Cardinals star Stan Musial got which nickname from Brooklyn fans in 1946?
questions.fact: Brooklyn fans groaned 'Here comes that man again' whenever he came up to bat at Ebbets Field.

questions.question: Which whistled tune became the Harlem Globetrotters' theme song in 1952?
options: Take Me Out to the Ball Game
questions.fact: The team plays it during its famous 'Magic Circle' warm-up, with tricky passes and ball spinning.

questions.question: Which famous Memorial Day car race returned in 1946 after being stopped for the war?
questions.fact: The Speedway sat empty and run-down during the war. Indiana businessman Tony Hulman bought it in 1945 and saved it.

questions.question: Maurice 'Rocket' Richard starred for which hockey team?
questions.fact: In the 1944–45 season he became the first player to score 50 goals in 50 games.

questions.question: In which Pennsylvania town was the first Little League World Series played, in 1947?
questions.fact: It was played on a small field on West Fourth Street. The series is still held every August in the Williamsport area.

questions.question: Which teenage tennis star, nicknamed 'Little Mo,' won all four major titles in 1953?
questions.fact: She was the first woman to win the Grand Slam, and she did it at just 18 years old.

questions.question: Who became the oldest heavyweight boxing champion up to that time when he won the title in 1951 at age 37?
questions.fact: He had lost four earlier title fights before finally winning the crown by knockout.

questions.question: At the 1952 Olympics, which Czech runner won the 5,000 meters, 10,000 meters and the marathon?
questions.fact: It was the first marathon he had ever run. His nickname was 'the Czech Locomotive.'

questions.question: Which team moved from St. Louis in 1954 to become the Baltimore Orioles?
questions.fact: The Browns had won just one American League pennant in over 50 years in St. Louis.

questions.question: In 1953, the Boston Braves moved to which city, the first big-league team move in 50 years?
questions.fact: Fans packed the new stadium, and the Braves set a National League attendance record in their very first season.

questions.question: In 1945, golfer Byron Nelson set a record by winning how many tournaments in a row?
questions.fact: He won 18 tournaments that year in all. Both records still stand.

questions.question: Which team won the first season of the league that became the NBA, in 1947?
questions.fact: Their star, 'Jumping Joe' Fulks, led the league in scoring with his new jump shot.

questions.question: Pitcher Satchel Paige became the oldest rookie in big-league history in 1948. Which team signed him?
questions.fact: He was 42 and had starred for years in the Negro leagues. Cleveland won the World Series that fall.

questions.question: What 1948 American program helped rebuild Europe after the war?
questions.fact: It sent billions of dollars to help rebuild homes, factories and farms across Europe.

questions.question: Which war hero was elected President of the United States in 1952?
questions.fact: 'I Like Ike' became one of the best-remembered campaign slogans ever.

questions.question: Who was crowned Queen in a famous 1953 ceremony at Westminster Abbey?
questions.fact: Millions watched on television, and many families bought their first TV set just to see it.

questions.question: After World War II, the U.S. and the Soviet Union became rivals in what was called the ___ War.
questions.fact: It was called 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.

questions.question: Which world organization was founded in 1945 to help keep the peace?
questions.fact: It started with 51 member countries. Today it has 193.

questions.question: Which country surrendered in May 1945, ending World War II in Europe?
questions.fact: May 8 became V-E Day, Victory in Europe Day, with joyful crowds in New York, London and Paris.

questions.question: What was the huge rise in births called that began in 1946, after soldiers came home?
questions.fact: Children born from 1946 to 1964 became known as the Baby Boomers, the biggest generation America had ever seen.

questions.question: In 1947, a pilot reported strange objects flying near Mount Rainier. What did newspapers call them?
questions.fact: Pilot Kenneth Arnold said they moved like a saucer skipping across water, and reporters coined the term 'flying saucer.'

questions.question: The Chicago Tribune's famous 1948 headline wrongly said which candidate had won the election?
questions.fact: The headline read 'Dewey Defeats Truman.' A grinning Truman held up the paper for photographers after his surprise win.

questions.question: In 1953, two climbers reached the top of Mount Everest for the first time. Who was one of them?
questions.fact: Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the top on May 29, 1953. The news reached London on the morning of the Queen's coronation.

questions.question: Whose polio vaccine was tested on schoolchildren across America in 1954?
questions.fact: About 1.8 million children took part and were called 'Polio Pioneers.' In 1955 the vaccine was declared safe and effective.

questions.question: The first 'Peanuts' comic strip ran in October 1950. Which character appeared in it?
questions.fact: Charles Schulz wanted to call it 'Li'l Folks.' The newspaper syndicate renamed it 'Peanuts,' a name he never liked.

questions.question: In a 1946 speech in Missouri, Winston Churchill said what had come down across Europe?
questions.fact: He gave the speech at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman sitting on the stage.

questions.question: Test pilot Chuck Yeager broke what barrier on October 14, 1947?
questions.fact: He flew the Bell X-1 rocket plane, which he named 'Glamorous Glennis' after his wife.

questions.question: When the Soviets blocked roads to West Berlin in 1948, how did the Allies get food and fuel to the city?
questions.fact: Planes landed around the clock for over a year. Pilot Gail Halvorsen dropped candy to children on tiny parachutes.

questions.question: NATO was founded in April 1949. What does NATO stand for?
questions.fact: It began with 12 countries, including the United States and Canada. An attack on one member counts as an attack on all.

questions.question: Which author's 1949 novel '1984' gave the world the all-seeing 'Big Brother'?
questions.fact: The book also gave us words like 'doublethink' and 'thought police.'

questions.question: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick described the 'double helix' shape of what?
questions.fact: Their paper was only about one page long. X-ray pictures made by Rosalind Franklin were key to the discovery.

questions.question: Which 1954 Supreme Court ruling said public schools could no longer be separated by race?
questions.fact: All nine justices agreed. The case was named for Oliver Brown, a father in Topeka, Kansas.

questions.question: In 1947, President Truman pledged aid to Greece and Turkey. What was this policy called?
questions.fact: He announced it in a speech to Congress in March 1947, promising to support free nations.

questions.question: Which amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits presidents to two terms?
questions.fact: It came after Franklin Roosevelt was elected four times, more than any other president.

questions.question: Princess Elizabeth became Queen in 1952 while on a trip to Kenya. How old was she?
questions.fact: She went on to reign for 70 years, the longest of any British monarch.

questions.question: In Richard Nixon's famous 1952 'Checkers' speech on TV, who or what was Checkers?
questions.fact: Checkers was a black and white cocker spaniel. Nixon's young daughter Tricia named him.

questions.question: Which First Lady, who moved into the White House in 1953, was famous for her love of the color pink?
questions.fact: She had White House rooms redecorated in her favorite colors, pink and green, and was known for her short bangs.

questions.question: Which two words were added to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954?
questions.fact: President Eisenhower signed the change into law on Flag Day, June 14, 1954.

questions.question: A sailor kissing a nurse in Times Square became the famous photo of which 1945 celebration?
questions.fact: Alfred Eisenstaedt took the picture for Life magazine as crowds celebrated the end of the war.

questions.question: Which president kept a sign on his desk that read 'The buck stops here'?
questions.fact: It meant he would not pass the blame to anyone else. A friend had the sign made at a federal reformatory in Oklahoma.

questions.question: Which folk artist was famous by 1949 for cheerful farm paintings she began making in her late 70s?
questions.fact: Anna Mary Robertson Moses kept painting until she was over 100. President Truman gave her an award in 1949.

questions.question: Dr. Benjamin Spock's huge 1946 bestseller gave parents advice about what?
questions.fact: It opened with the reassuring words 'Trust yourself. You know more than you think you do.'

questions.question: Which doodle of a big-nosed man peeking over a wall was drawn everywhere by GIs in the 1940s?
questions.fact: It came with the words 'Kilroy was here.' Soldiers drew it on walls all over the world.

questions.question: President Eisenhower loved which sport so much that he had a practice green put in at the White House?
questions.fact: Golf was his favorite way to relax. He practiced his putting just outside the Oval Office.

questions.question: ENIAC, unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946, was one of the first what?
questions.fact: It filled a large room, weighed about 30 tons and used around 18,000 vacuum tubes.

questions.question: In 1953, Eisenhower renamed the presidential retreat in Maryland after his grandson. What is it called?
questions.fact: Franklin Roosevelt had called it 'Shangri-La.' The grandson, David Eisenhower, later married Richard Nixon's daughter Julie.

questions.question: Harry Truman became president in April 1945. Which state was he from?
questions.fact: He grew up in Independence, Missouri, and once ran a men's clothing store in Kansas City.

questions.question: Which wealthy American gave the land in New York City for the United Nations headquarters in 1946?
questions.fact: He paid $8.5 million for the land along the East River. Before that, the site was mostly slaughterhouses.

questions.question: The Philippines gained independence from the United States in 1946 on which date?
questions.fact: In 1962 the Philippines moved its Independence Day to June 12, the date of its earlier declaration from Spain.

questions.question: On election night 1952, CBS used a new machine called UNIVAC to predict the winner. What was UNIVAC?
questions.fact: It predicted an Eisenhower landslide from early returns. The experts did not trust it at first, but it was right.

questions.question: In 1951, people in Englewood, New Jersey, became the first to do what without an operator?
questions.fact: The town's mayor made the first call, to the mayor of Alameda, California.

questions.question: Which former governor of California became Chief Justice of the United States in 1953?
questions.fact: He led the Supreme Court for 16 years. He had also been the Republican candidate for vice president in 1948.

questions.question: Whose 1949 presidential inauguration was the first one shown on television?
questions.fact: It was also the first inauguration to be broadcast with sound and pictures to millions across the country.

questions.question: From 1949 to 1952 the Trumans lived across the street at Blair House. Why?
questions.fact: The old building was so weak that a leg of Margaret Truman's piano had broken through the floor.

questions.question: When West Germany was formed in 1949, which small city on the Rhine became its capital?
questions.fact: It stayed the capital until Germany reunited in 1990. Bonn is also where Beethoven was born.

questions.question: Harry Truman called his program for housing, jobs and health the 'Fair' what?
questions.fact: He laid out the Fair Deal in his January 1949 State of the Union address.

questions.question: In 1952, which American ocean liner crossed the Atlantic faster than any passenger ship before?
questions.fact: It made the trip in about three and a half days and won the Blue Riband, the honor for the fastest Atlantic crossing.

questions.question: The 1950 census counted about how many people in the United States?
questions.fact: The exact count was 151,325,798, up 14.5 percent from 1940. New York was the most populous state.

questions.question: Which United Nations agency, founded in 1948, marks its birthday every April 7?
questions.fact: The day is celebrated each year as World Health Day.

questions.question: In 1952, which US island territory approved its own constitution and became a commonwealth?
questions.fact: Its constitution took effect on July 25, 1952. Luis Muñoz Marín was its first elected governor.

questions.question: In 1950, President Truman wrote an angry letter to a music critic who had panned whose singing?
questions.fact: Margaret Truman was a concert singer. The critic, Paul Hume, wrote for the Washington Post.

questions.question: In 1949, New York jeweler Harry Winston bought which famous blue diamond?
questions.fact: He later gave it to the Smithsonian, sending it by ordinary registered mail in a plain package.

questions.question: In 1949, which island joined Canada as its tenth province?
questions.fact: It had been a separate British dominion. Its people voted in 1948 to join Canada.

questions.question: Starting in 1952, what did Lucy in 'Peanuts' keep pulling away just as Charlie Brown tried to kick it?
questions.fact: Charles Schulz drew the gag nearly every fall for decades, and Charlie Brown never once got to kick the ball.

questions.question: In 1940s slang, if someone called you a 'dreamboat,' what did they mean?
questions.fact: Teenagers used it for their favorite crooners and movie stars, and for the cutest boy or girl in school.

questions.question: In the slang of the day, if something was 'the cat's meow,' what was it?
questions.fact: It could also mean a fancy, sought-after thing, like a shiny new car everybody wanted.

questions.question: In 1950s slang, what was a 'square'?
questions.fact: The opposite of a square was someone 'hip' or 'cool' who kept up with the latest fads.

questions.question: In 1950s teen slang, what did 'wheels' mean?
questions.fact: Having your own wheels meant freedom: drive-ins, sock hops and cruising Main Street on a Saturday night.

questions.question: About how much did a new 1946 Chevrolet cost?
questions.fact: The list price was $1,076. Car factories had built tanks and planes during the war, so buyers lined up for the first new cars in years.

questions.question: What was the typical value of an American home in 1950?
questions.fact: The census found the middle value was $7,354. By the year 2000 it had climbed to $119,600.

questions.question: About how much did a gallon of regular gas cost in 1950, taxes included?
questions.fact: The national average was 26.8 cents a gallon. A full tank cost about four dollars.

questions.question: How much did it cost to mail a letter with a first-class stamp in 1947?
questions.fact: The 3-cent rate lasted from 1932 all the way to 1958.

questions.question: Which 1940s exclamation was a cheeky way of saying someone looked very attractive?
questions.fact: It was a strong, playful compliment, and you can still hear it today, usually said with a wink.

questions.question: In 1950s slang, who would you call 'Daddy-O'?
questions.fact: It was a friendly, hip way to address any man, not just your dad.

questions.question: In 1940s jazz slang, a 'hep cat' was someone who was what?
questions.fact: Hep cats were fans of swing and bebop jazz. 'Hep' later turned into 'hip,' and our game's Hepcats team is named after them.

questions.question: Nylon stockings were hard to find during the war. What was the nylon needed for instead?
questions.fact: When they came back in stores, huge lines formed. In Pittsburgh in 1946, about 40,000 people lined up for 13,000 pairs.

questions.question: Builder William Levitt started his famous low-cost suburb, Levittown, in 1947 in which state?
questions.fact: Crews built the houses assembly-line style, moving from lot to lot and doing one job at each house.

questions.question: In 1940s slang, if everything was 'copacetic,' how were things?
questions.fact: Tap dancer Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson helped make the word popular.

questions.question: Only two of which small German cars were sold in the United States in 1949, their first year here?
questions.fact: Few people wanted the odd little car at first. Twenty years later it was the best-selling imported car in America.

questions.question: The FBI started its 'Ten Most Wanted' list in 1950. Who was running the FBI?
questions.fact: J. Edgar Hoover led the FBI for 48 years, under eight presidents.

questions.question: What new convenience meal did Swanson introduce in 1953?
questions.fact: The first one was turkey with cornbread dressing, peas and sweet potatoes in an aluminum tray.

questions.question: When Mr. Potato Head first came out in 1952, what did children stick his eyes and nose into?
questions.fact: He was the first toy ever advertised on television. A plastic potato body came along in 1964.

questions.question: Which spring toy that 'walks' down stairs first went on sale in 1945?
questions.fact: Engineer Richard James invented it. At its first demonstration, at Gimbels in Philadelphia, 400 sold in about 90 minutes.

questions.question: Which stretchy, bouncy toy went on sale in 1950, packed inside a plastic egg?
questions.fact: It was discovered by accident when wartime scientists were trying to make fake rubber.

questions.question: Which crossword-style board game took off so fast in 1952 that its maker couldn't keep up with orders?
questions.fact: Its inventor, an out-of-work architect named Alfred Butts, first called it 'Criss-Crosswords.'

questions.question: Which children's board game, first sold in 1949, has a path through a land of sweets?
questions.fact: Teacher Eleanor Abbott designed it while recovering from polio, to entertain children in the hospital.

questions.question: Which candy's 1954 slogan was 'melts in your mouth, not in your hand'?
questions.fact: The hard candy shell kept the chocolate from melting. M&M's were first made for soldiers because they traveled well.

questions.question: Which plastic food containers, later famous for home sales parties, were introduced in 1946?
questions.fact: Earl Tupper invented the 'burping' seal. Saleswoman Brownie Wise made the home parties a sensation.

questions.question: In 1948, what new kind of camera went on sale that made its own prints in about a minute?
questions.fact: Edwin Land's Model 95 Land Camera is widely considered the first instant camera sold to the public.

questions.question: Which laundry detergent from Procter & Gamble first went on sale in 1946?
questions.fact: Procter & Gamble had sold a gentler synthetic soap, Dreft, since 1933, mostly for washing baby clothes.

questions.question: At 1950s drive-ins, what were the servers called who brought food out to your car?
questions.fact: Many carhops zipped from car to car on roller skates, balancing trays that hooked onto the car window.

questions.question: Stores like Woolworth's, full of cheap odds and ends, were nicknamed what?
questions.fact: They were also called dime stores. F. W. Woolworth's was the most famous chain of them all.

questions.question: What were teenage girls of the 1940s called, after the ankle socks they wore?
questions.fact: They were famous for screaming and swooning over young Frank Sinatra.

questions.question: Which dog was a favorite decoration on the felt circle skirts that girls wore in the early 1950s?
questions.fact: Juli Lynne Charlot made the first one in 1947 for a Christmas party, because she couldn't sew and felt needed no seams.

questions.question: Which cartoon tiger was introduced in 1952 to sell Sugar Frosted Flakes?
questions.fact: His famous line is 'They're gr-r-reat!' For decades he was voiced by Thurl Ravenscroft.

questions.question: Which new writing tool sold out at Gimbels in New York in 1945, at $12.50 each?
questions.fact: That was a lot of money then. Shoppers crowded the store on the first day to see a pen that wrote without an inkwell.

questions.question: Which charge card, launched in 1950, could first be used only at restaurants in New York?
questions.fact: Founder Frank McNamara got the idea after he went to dinner and forgot his wallet.

questions.question: The first Holiday Inn opened in Memphis in 1952. What was it named after?
questions.fact: Founder Kemmons Wilson was fed up with cramped, pricey motels on a family road trip, so he built his own.

questions.question: In 1948, the McDonald brothers reopened their California burger stand with a fast new system. What did they call it?
questions.fact: They cut the menu down to nine items and made burgers assembly-line style.

questions.question: The first Pillsbury Bake-Off was held in 1949 at which famous New York hotel?
questions.fact: Contestants baked their recipes in the hotel's grand ballroom. Eleanor Roosevelt was a guest at the very first one.

questions.question: Which frozen seafood dinner favorite did Birds Eye bring to American stores in 1953?
questions.fact: They were sold as an easy, mess-free way to serve fish, perfect for Friday dinners.

questions.question: The first Chevrolet Corvette of 1953 had a body made of what?
questions.fact: Only 300 were made that first year, every one of them white with a red interior.

questions.question: Because of its flat, boxy sides, the 1949 Ford got which nickname?
questions.fact: It was Ford's first all-new car after the war. Its fenders blended into the body instead of sticking out.

questions.question: Northland Center, one of the first big shopping malls, opened in 1954 near which city?
questions.fact: Architect Victor Gruen designed it. He went on to design the first fully enclosed mall in 1956.

questions.question: Which French designer's 1947 'New Look' brought back long, full skirts and tiny waists?
questions.fact: Harper's Bazaar editor Carmel Snow gave the style its name at Dior's very first show, in February 1947.

questions.question: In 1951, which carmaker became the first to offer power steering on a passenger car?
questions.fact: It came on the 1951 Chrysler Imperial and was called 'Hydraguide.'

questions.question: In 1945, engineer Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near radar equipment. What did that lead to?
questions.fact: The first microwave ovens were nearly six feet tall and were sold to restaurants. They were called 'Radaranges.'

questions.question: In 1952, which Kentucky colonel sold his very first restaurant franchise for fried chicken?
questions.fact: The first franchise went to Pete Harman in South Salt Lake, Utah, a long way from Kentucky.

questions.question: Which doughnut chain opened its first shop in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1950?
questions.fact: Founder William Rosenberg had first called his shop 'Open Kettle' before choosing the new name.

questions.question: Which spreadable cheese sauce in a jar did Kraft bring out in 1953?
questions.fact: It was created by a team led by food scientist Edwin Traisman.

questions.question: Ice cream chain Baskin-Robbins became famous for how many flavors, one for each day of the month?
questions.fact: Burt Baskin and Irv Robbins were brothers-in-law who joined their ice cream shops together in 1953.

questions.question: Which brand of frozen orange juice concentrate, launched in 1946, was promoted by Bing Crosby?
questions.fact: Bing Crosby was an early investor, and he plugged the juice on his radio show.

questions.question: In-N-Out Burger opened in 1948 near Los Angeles with what new feature?
questions.fact: Customers ordered through a two-way speaker without leaving their cars, one of the first drive-thrus of its kind.
